book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book

chapters.file: ch18 - Human Rights, Human Nature, and Amistad.md
chapters.relation: Baggett and Foreman use Amistad to reconstruct Locke's theory of natural rights: Cinque's mutiny and John Quincy Adams's Supreme Court plea that man's natural state is freedom illustrate Locke's claim that God's workmanship makes us his property and therefore un-ownable by other men. They contrast Locke's voluntarist natural law with Aquinas's, note Adams rebutting the Hobbesian 'war of all against all' quoted in the pro-slavery Executive Review, and invoke Mill's perfect/imperfect duty distinction (Baldwin's obligation to his clients) plus Bentham's rights-denying utilitarianism, which they map onto Calhoun's warning about the cost of abolition.

chapters.file: ch19 - Terrorism, Counterterrorism, and “The Story of What Happens Next” in Munich.md
chapters.relation: Foy reads Munich's Operation Wrath of God as Spielberg's argument for retribution over vengeance in state counterterrorism. Yvonne's Marcuse/Hegel relativism and the agents' 'think of yourself as a soldier' language-games are dismissed as Avner's psychological breakdown shows morality is objective. Foy deploys Nozick's five procedural differences between retribution and revenge and Kant's view of retribution as impersonal and rational, echoes Socrates in the Crito (retaliation harms one's own soul) via Avner's decay, and cites Aristotle's 'war for the sake of peace' and jus in bello discrimination/proportionality in the Hamshari and Jeanette assassinations.

chapters.file: ch20 - Part III Realism, Mind, and Metaphysics.md

chapters.relation: Dromm proposes three criteria for cinematic realism—disguised representation, fidelity to the real world, and emotional response—drawing on Saving Private Ryan's desaturated handheld Normandy footage, Schindler's List's black and white, Jurassic Park's dinosaurs, and Minority Report's plausible future tech. He answers Bertolt Brecht's Marxist objection that empathy dulls the audience's critical, world-changing capacity (Brecht echoing Marx's Theses on Feuerbach) by arguing, via Amistad's 'who they are' and Saving Private Ryan, that empathetic understanding of others' feelings is itself the strongest motive for humane action.

chapters.file: ch22 - A.I. Artificial Intelligence Artistic Indulgence or Advanced Inquiry.md
chapters.relation: White argues A.I. dramatizes the mind-body problem through the mecha child David, proposing a 'Strengthened Turing Test' (STT) in which the audience knows he is a machine yet must judge whether he truly loves Monica. He runs Searle's Chinese Room (David as mere rule-follower with no qualia) against Nagel's 'what is it like' and Chalmers's zombie argument and property-dualist multiple realizability, which would let a sufficiently complex David be genuinely conscious. White contends the imprinting device—David's built-in need for one other being—is what lets him pass the STT, sidestepping Cartesian dualism's interaction problem.

chapters.file: ch23 - Minority Report, Molinism, and the Viability of Precrime.md
chapters.relation: Kowalski defends the conceptual coherence of Minority Report's Precrime by dissolving the freedom-vs-foreknowledge worry: the precogs' prevision of Howard Marks knifing his wife shows only that 'necessarily, if it is foreknown, it happens,' not that the act happens necessarily, so contingency and free choice survive (Anderton's rolling-ball demo and Agatha's 'You can choose!'). He recasts the precogs' power as Luis de Molina's knowledge of the conditional future (middle knowledge)—Agatha narrating the life Sean never lived—invoking Aristotle, Augustine, Boethius, Aquinas, and Ockham on the problem, and finally rejects Spielberg's shut-it-down stance as a fallacious slippery-slope argument.

chapters.file: ch24 - Appendix Discussing Five Spielberg Films.md
chapters.relation: This appendix is not an argumentative essay but a teaching aid: it gives roughly 1,000-1,500-word plot summaries of Schindler's List, Amistad, A.I., Minority Report, and Munich, each followed by discussion questions. The questions gesture at the volume's philosophical themes—moral objectivism vs relativism about the Holocaust, Locke-style natural rights and unjust law in Amistad, whether an android can love in A.I., the justice of infallible Precrime, and the ethics of counterterrorist vengeance in Munich—but the appendix itself advances no thesis and applies no single philosopher, instead prompting readers to consult the companion essays.

holes.name: Cinematic Realism
holes.what: The aesthetic theory of what makes a film realistic—disguised representation, fidelity to reality, and the illusion that grounds emotional response—as developed by Bazin, Perkins, and Goodman.
holes.why: Chapter 21 is entirely about defining and defending cinematic realism as a philosophy-of-art thesis, and no existing taxonomy concept captures film/representational realism.

holes.name: Middle Knowledge (Molinism)
holes.what: Molina's doctrine that God (or any knower) can know the conditional future—what a free agent would freely choose in any fully specified circumstance—prior to and independent of that agent's actual choice.
holes.why: Chapter 23's central move is recasting the precogs' power as Molinist knowledge of the conditional future, and neither Molina nor middle knowledge exists in the taxonomy.

holes.name: Luis de Molina
holes.what: 16th-century Spanish Jesuit whose Concordia (1588) introduced middle knowledge to reconcile divine providence and foreknowledge with human free will.
holes.why: Molina is the named philosophical anchor of chapter 23 ('Minority Report, Molinism...') and is used substantively, but he is absent from the taxonomy's philosopher list.
